I have been working these fields for 40 years, so I know my land well. My 16.1 mu is mostly good loam with irrigation from the well, which gives me flexibility most of my neighbors without wells don't have.

I split my land this way: about 3 mu of cotton on the plot furthest from the house — that ground is a bit sandier and cotton tolerates it better. The remaining 13.1 mu stays in my wheat-maize double crop, which is the backbone of any Quzhou farm.

**Winter wheat (13.1 mu):** I already planted last October. I use an improved variety — Jimai 22 or something similar — because the old local seed can't match the yields. I apply about 18 kg/mu of pure N split between base fertilizer and top-dressing at jointing. Phosphorus I put all at sowing, around 8 kg/mu as P₂O₅. Potassium 6 kg/mu — our soil has some native K but not enough. I irrigate 4 times: overwintering, green-up/jointing, heading, and grain-filling. Pesticide 2 times — once for aphids and once for powdery mildew if I see it. I aim for 500 kg/mu; in a good year I hit 550.

**Summer maize (13.1 mu):** Right after wheat harvest in June, I no-till sow hybrid maize (Zhengdan 958 or Denghai type) with the seeder — saves time and moisture. N about 16 kg/mu, mostly side-dressed at big-trumpet stage because early N just leaches. P 6 kg/mu, K 6 kg/mu with the starter. Irrigate twice — after sowing if dry, and at tasseling. Two sprays: one for corn borer, one for armyworm if pressure is high. 550 kg/mu is realistic.

**Cotton (3 mu):** Spring planting in late April. I use improved Bt cotton — the bollworm problem is much smaller now than 20 years ago, but I still need to spray for aphids, mites, and plant bugs. N 14 kg/mu, P 7 kg/mu, K 10 kg/mu because cotton is a potassium-hungry crop and my yield drops if I skimp. Plough once in spring — cotton needs a deeper seedbed than maize. Irrigate 3 times. Pesticide about 6 times through the season. I expect 240 kg seed cotton/mu.

I keep my rates a little above the minimum because a bad yield costs far more than a few extra bags of fertilizer. But I am not wasteful — I learned years ago that over-applying N on wheat just makes it lodge.
